virals.name: Doreen
virals.text:
Pika H3 Flex is here, and I put it to work on a tiny, ridiculous film.

I gave a tiny lavender octopus an impossible claw-machine challenge in a rain-soaked arcade. Neon reflections, a curious seagull, frantic joystick corrections, one lucky double grab, and an over-the-top victory dance turned a simple prompt into a miniature cinematic comedy.

What stands out is the room to iterate. H3 Flex supports text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video workflows, with precise editing for characters, camera moves, looks, and voices.

You can work from up to 12 references, separate the result into up to five audio stems, and move from a 768p draft to 4K finishing.

More room to experiment, refine, and keep the details that make a generation feel like a film.

virals.name: Jonah Bennett
virals.text:
Notes from the 2nd Annual AI Film Festival Japan

There were 730 short film submissions this year, 68 selections, and 21 finalists.

My biggest takeaway from the submissions was the sheer range of what's now possible. Almost anything you can imagine can be generated in almost any aesthetic.

Some other thoughts: 

- There were at least a couple of films that were so well done that the average viewer would not have known they were AI. Almost none of the films hit that mark, but a couple did. Impressive stuff. I expect the models to improve significantly for next year, both voice and video. 

-  Submission quality varied greatly. A lot of the selections shouldn’t have made the cut at all, which makes you wonder about the quality of the hundreds of submissions that weren’t selected. One even left in a watermark for the whole film. 

- Directors with actual film industry experience/education created much more professional content. There are a lot of subtleties that go into film production, which is still true with AI films. They require a huge amount of cross-domain knowledge to produce something watchable. You have to be good at sound design, music, script writing, storyboarding, visuals, voiceovers, editing, etc. I saw a lot of flubs in one or more of those dimensions. If you want to generate great AI films, you have to do a whole lot more than just learning how to prompt. 

- AI video generation won't save you from tropes like "it was all just a dream/nightmare," "let's use AI generated video content to talk about AI," "dead wife or similar", etc.

- Voices and faces are becoming more natural-looking and emotionally expressive, at least in the better films. 

- It’s very clear when someone is using old models, and when they’re lacking in skill. Those kinds of submissions sound almost exactly like those annoying, AI-generated YouTube ads that want to scam you into buying a course about corporate communication skills.  

- The highest quality video generation came from seedance, and it wasn’t close. 

- Character consistency is more or less a solved problem, and where I noticed some issues, they were relatively minor and didn’t ruin anything. If the story is good, you can ignore some glitches, just like we’ve been ignoring bad CGI for decades.  

-  AI hasn’t mastered the art of crying/tears yet. 

- One of the directors generated their film in about 6 hours, from concept to finish. That was probably the fastest. Others took a couple weeks, or a couple months. Wide range in time spent.

outsiders.name: Doreen
outsiders.text:
Pika H3 Flex is here, and I put it to work on a tiny, ridiculous film.

I gave a tiny lavender octopus an impossible claw-machine challenge in a rain-soaked arcade. Neon reflections, a curious seagull, frantic joystick corrections, one lucky double grab, and an over-the-top victory dance turned a simple prompt into a miniature cinematic comedy.

What stands out is the room to iterate. H3 Flex supports text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video workflows, with precise editing for characters, camera moves, looks, and voices.

You can work from up to 12 references, separate the result into up to five audio stems, and move from a 768p draft to 4K finishing.

More room to experiment, refine, and keep the details that make a generation feel like a film.

outsiders.name: Jonah Bennett
outsiders.text:
Notes from the 2nd Annual AI Film Festival Japan

There were 730 short film submissions this year, 68 selections, and 21 finalists.

My biggest takeaway from the submissions was the sheer range of what's now possible. Almost anything you can imagine can be generated in almost any aesthetic.

Some other thoughts: 

- There were at least a couple of films that were so well done that the average viewer would not have known they were AI. Almost none of the films hit that mark, but a couple did. Impressive stuff. I expect the models to improve significantly for next year, both voice and video. 

-  Submission quality varied greatly. A lot of the selections shouldn’t have made the cut at all, which makes you wonder about the quality of the hundreds of submissions that weren’t selected. One even left in a watermark for the whole film. 

- Directors with actual film industry experience/education created much more professional content. There are a lot of subtleties that go into film production, which is still true with AI films. They require a huge amount of cross-domain knowledge to produce something watchable. You have to be good at sound design, music, script writing, storyboarding, visuals, voiceovers, editing, etc. I saw a lot of flubs in one or more of those dimensions. If you want to generate great AI films, you have to do a whole lot more than just learning how to prompt. 

- AI video generation won't save you from tropes like "it was all just a dream/nightmare," "let's use AI generated video content to talk about AI," "dead wife or similar", etc.

- Voices and faces are becoming more natural-looking and emotionally expressive, at least in the better films. 

- It’s very clear when someone is using old models, and when they’re lacking in skill. Those kinds of submissions sound almost exactly like those annoying, AI-generated YouTube ads that want to scam you into buying a course about corporate communication skills.  

- The highest quality video generation came from seedance, and it wasn’t close. 

- Character consistency is more or less a solved problem, and where I noticed some issues, they were relatively minor and didn’t ruin anything. If the story is good, you can ignore some glitches, just like we’ve been ignoring bad CGI for decades.  

-  AI hasn’t mastered the art of crying/tears yet. 

- One of the directors generated their film in about 6 hours, from concept to finish. That was probably the fastest. Others took a couple weeks, or a couple months. Wide range in time spent.

x_keywords.method: Read-only x MCP search_posts_all, 2 calls per keyword: last 24 h and previous 24 h (24-48 h ago); lang:en, no retweets/replies, sort=relevancy, up to 25 posts per window. This is a SAMPLE of top-relevance posts, not every post on X. Views = impression_count at fetch time. Rank = sum of sampled 24 h views; 48 h = both windows; trend = 24 h sum / previous 24 h sum (up >=1.3, down <=0.7). Fresh posts are still gaining views, so 'up' is understated. Top-post share > 70% means one viral post carries the keyword.

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
